A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching systems, evaluation framework and retained COVID experiments. Text, tables, figures and all appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V3 reports original coding experiments comparing collaboration settings, quantitative theme-quality results, a 1,200-pair manual correctness evaluation and participant interviews.

after.justification: V5 retains the original empirical results and adds climate-advertising experiments and original comparative analyses of the two corpora.

M1.justification: The three interactive coding procedures, user interventions and core evaluation framework remain unchanged. The QDTM initialization and Llama model specified in v5's main text already appear in v3's appendices; the new corpus diagnostics do not establish a coding-method change.

E1.justification: V5 adds evaluation on 5,471 English-language US climate advertisements alongside the retained COVID-vaccine tweets, using all three systems and both collaboration settings. This substantially broadens domain and document-genre coverage beyond the original short social-media posts.

E2.justification: The evaluated systems remain Fang et al. (2023)'s topic model, Pacheco et al. (2023)'s relational system and Chew et al. (2023)'s LLM framework. The climate comparisons extend this same set; no comparator is added or removed within the retained experiments.

E3.justification: The reported participant pool increases from 20 to 33. Appendix A introduces a substantial corpus-analysis protocol covering readability, lexical diversity, template clustering and semantic diagnostics, including 5,000-document samples for template analysis. The original coding-group configuration and 1,200-pair correctness audit remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 5.4 and Appendix A investigate corpus characteristics that might explain differing collaboration outcomes, including linguistic complexity, formulaic repetition, n-grams, theme ambiguity and semantic similarity distributions. The existing top-quartile cohesiveness analysis and correctness-by-distance analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A adds statistical testing and effect-size reporting for corpus differences, including a Mann–Whitney U test for document length with p<0.001 and r=-0.353. Existing unpaired t-tests, significance thresholds and correctness-annotation agreement reporting remain unchanged; no additional seed or repeated-run reporting is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 add climate results: topic-model Jaccard consistency is 0.37 synchronously versus 0.58 asynchronously, contrasting with the retained COVID values of 0.56 versus 0.30. Appendix A adds extensive corpus-analysis results. These are new results under different data conditions; the original COVID tables, correctness figure and LLM prompt-selection results are retained.

T1.justification: The definitions and calculations underlying consistency, cohesiveness and distinctiveness retain their meaning. Neither version presents theoretical proofs, and v5's additional empirical diagnostics introduce no substantive formal derivation, assumption or theorem.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions concerning collaboration effects and a common evaluation framework are retained. The introduction adds a third research question about dataset characteristics and explicitly broadens the claimed demonstration to effects across different datasets.

C2.justification: V5 adds corpus-dependent explanations and recommendations: complex, diverse corpora may favor asynchronous reflection, while homogeneous corpora may suit synchronous discussion. It also removes v3's explicit cautions about automated-versus-human evaluation disagreement and limited human validation, replacing the single-dataset limitation with a broader acknowledgment of nonexhaustive coverage.

D1.justification: V5 newly documents repeat-participant ordering, corpus-analysis methods and thresholds, and an explicit artifact-licensing statement. The QDTM settings, Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct model, hardware, compute information and prompt templates match v3's appendices; their restatement in the main text is not new implementation information.

R1.justification: V5 adds Baden et al. (2022) to motivate attention to dataset diversity and Islam et al. (2023) for the climate corpus. The remaining cited works and the central positioning as a shared evaluation framework for existing interactive coding tools are retained.

P1.justification: The introduction, consistency explanation and user-study discussion are substantially rewritten and condensed. V5 introduces numbered subsections throughout Sections 3–5, adds the dataset-differences discussion and appendix, reorganizes the limitations and appendices, and changes author ordering and some terminology.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 are restructured with separate COVID and Climate groups, and six new appendix tables display corpus characteristics and diagnostics. Existing appendix tables are relocated and renumbered. All four figure images are unchanged, although captions are edited, including an explicit COVID qualification for Figure 4.

improvement.justification: The climate evaluation reduces v3's single-corpus limitation and reveals dataset-dependent consistency patterns, making the applicability discussion more informative (Tables 1–2 and Section 5.4). Benefits are tempered by retained COVID-only human correctness validation, removal of the earlier validation caveat, and a new reporting contradiction: Table 8 labels similarity >0.3 while its accompanying prose says below 0.3. The broader evidence supports a limited net improvement.
